title: Statistics for AI
learning_outcomes: Explain statistics for AI and connect at least two of its listed subtopics.
Apply the central idea in statistics for AI to a small example or select a suitable approach for a stated scenario.
Identify an important assumption, failure mode, risk, or limitation and describe how it should be checked.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study statistics for AI within Mathematical and Computational Foundations. You will connect the syllabus topics below to a small, inspectable example and practice stating what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Mathematical and computational ideas make model behavior easier to reason about. Start with small values, explicit assumptions, and readable calculations.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Descriptive statistics summarize a sample, while inferential methods reason from observed data toward a broader population with uncertainty. Sample selection, spread, confounding, and measurement choices can change the conclusion.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics covered in this lesson

items.title: Mean, median, and mode
items.text: Summary statistics describe different properties of a sample: center and spread are distinct, and outliers may change them differently. Report sample size and inspect the distribution rather than relying on one number.

items.title: Variance and standard deviation
items.text: Summary statistics describe different properties of a sample: center and spread are distinct, and outliers may change them differently. Report sample size and inspect the distribution rather than relying on one number.

items.title: Sampling and populations
items.text: A sample is the subset of records observed; the population is the group about which a conclusion is intended. Biased or unrepresentative sampling can limit generalization regardless of sample size.

items.title: Correlation and covariance
items.text: Summary statistics describe different properties of a sample: center and spread are distinct, and outliers may change them differently. Report sample size and inspect the distribution rather than relying on one number.

items.title: Statistical inference
items.text: Statistical inference is one of the concepts used to reason about statistics for ai. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

items.title: Confidence intervals and uncertainty
items.text: A confidence interval communicates sampling uncertainty under a specified statistical procedure and its assumptions. It is not a guarantee that an individual prediction is correct or that a particular interval has a fixed probability after observing it.

items.title: Recognizing misleading statistics
items.text: Recognizing misleading statistics is one of the concepts used to reason about statistics for ai. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: If the output differs, check indentation and spelling, confirm you saved the intended file, and compare each input value with the example. If the example runs as expected, do not infer that it proves a trained model works; this snippet is a deterministic teaching aid. Keep sensitive data out of tests.

content_blocks.title: Check before you trust a result
content_blocks.text: This is a small, deterministic teaching example—not a trained AI model or evidence of production performance. Run it with a local Python 3 interpreter; do not paste secrets or private data into experiments.

task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core concept and accurately refer to the source syllabus topics.

Document at least one limitation, safety consideration, or evaluation requirement.
hints: Write down the inputs, expected output, and assumptions before changing the example.
Change only one input or condition and compare the results with your original prediction.
Ask whether the example covers realistic cases, important subgroups, and failure conditions; a toy example does not establish production reliability.
troubleshooting: Use Python 3 and run the file from the folder where it was saved.
If output differs, restore the original input and compare one changed value at a time.
If Python reports a syntax error, check copied quotation marks, indentation, and whether the full code block was copied.
